summary.text: For \(k\ge 60\), set \(n=2k+1\); the assumed nonzero determinant forces some matrix entry to be nonzero, so its two labels \(p=n+i-j\) and \(q=n+j-i\) are prime and satisfy \(p+q=2n=4k+2\). The cases \(1\le k\le 59\) are covered by an explicit finite list of prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)=A228623(n)\). Thus, for each positive integer \(n\), let \(M_n\) be the \(n\times n\) integer matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and whose \((i,j)\)-entry is
\[
(M_n)_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Here the subtractions are natural-number subtractions. Because \(0\le i,j<n\), however, we have \(j<n\le n+i\) and \(i<n\le n+j\). Consequently neither subtraction is truncated: these quantities agree with the corresponding ordinary integer differences. By definition,
\[
a(n)=\det(M_n).
\]

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement
\[
H:\qquad n>120\text{ and }n\text{ odd}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(n)\ne0.
\]
We prove that, for every integer \(k>0\), the integer \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

Fix \(k>0\). We divide the proof into two cases.

**Case 1: \(k\ge 60\).**

Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd, and
\[
n=2k+1\ge 2\cdot60+1=121>120.
\]
The hypothesis \(H\) therefore gives
\[
\det(M_n)=a(n)\ne0.
\]

Since \(n\ge121\), the matrix has at least one row and column. If every entry of \(M_n\) were zero, then \(M_n\) would be the zero matrix and its determinant would be zero. This contradicts \(\det(M_n)\ne0\). Hence there are indices \(i,j\), with
\[
0\le i<n,\qquad 0\le j<n,
\]
such that \((M_n)_{ij}\ne0\). Every entry of \(M_n\) is either \(0\) or \(1\), so this entry must equal \(1\). By the definition of the matrix, the two natural numbers
\[
p=n+i-j,
\qquad
q=n+j-i
\]
are therefore prime.

It remains to compute their sum. The bounds on the indices imply
\[
j<n\le n+i,\qquad i<n\le n+j,
\]
so, as noted above, the two natural subtractions are exact. We may thus add them as ordinary integer differences:
\[
p+q=(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n.
\]
Using \(n=2k+1\), this becomes
\[
p+q=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
Thus \(4k+2\) is a sum of the two primes \(p\) and \(q\).

**Case 2: \(k<60\).**

Because \(k>0\), this means \(1\le k\le59\). These finitely many values are covered by the following table. In each row, the displayed numbers \(p,q\) are prime and their displayed sum is \(4k+2\).

For completeness, the distinct numbers used in the table are
\[
\begin{gathered}
3,5,7,11,13,19,23,31,37,43,47,53,59,61,67,71,73,79,83,89,97,\\
103,107,109,113,127,131,139,151,157,163,167,173,179,181,191,193,\\
199,211,223,227,229,233.
\end{gathered}
\]
Their primality follows directly by trial division: since all are at most \(233\), it suffices for each number to test possible prime divisors no larger than its square root, hence only among \(2,3,5,7,11,13\); none of the applicable divisors divides the number in question. The additions in the last column of each half of the table give exactly \(4k+2\), so the table proves every case \(1\le k\le59\).

The two cases exhaust all positive integers \(k\). Therefore, under the assumed nonvanishing conjecture for \(A228623\), for every \(k>0\) there exist primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
4k+2=p+q.
\]
This is the required Goldbach statement for even integers of the form \(4k+2\).
